Week 9 · Phase 3: Attention & Pretrained Models

The Transformer Architecture

Self-attention from first principles, multi-head attention with exact tensor shapes, feed-forward layers, residuals and normalization, positional encodings from sinusoids to RoPE and ALiBi, encoder/decoder variants and causal masking, the quadratic cost and its cures, parameter and FLOP counting, training tricks, and a from-scratch GPT in PyTorch.

76 min read4 interactive demos13 figures16 code blocks9 exercises
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you should be able to:

  • Derive scaled dot-product attention from the idea of a soft dictionary lookup, and prove why the 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_k}1/dk​​ factor keeps the softmax out of its saturated regime.
  • Write multi-head attention with exact tensor shapes at every step, and implement it in PyTorch without nn.MultiheadAttention.
  • Explain the roles of the position-wise feed-forward network, residual connections, layer normalization and RMSNorm, and argue when pre-norm is preferable to post-norm.
  • Compare sinusoidal, learned, relative, rotary (RoPE) and ALiBi position schemes, and derive why RoPE makes attention scores depend only on relative offsets.
  • Distinguish encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder models, and implement causal and padding masks correctly.
  • Count the parameters and FLOPs of a Transformer from its hyperparameters, explain the quadratic cost of attention, and compare sparse, sliding-window and linear attention.
  • Apply the standard training recipe (AdamW, warmup, label smoothing, mixed precision) and train a GPT-style decoder from scratch on a tiny corpus, then sample from it.

In Week 7 you saw attention as an add-on to a recurrent encoder-decoder: a decoder looked back at the encoder's hidden states with a learned weighted average. It worked so well that a natural question arose. If attention lets every output position reach every input position directly, what is the recurrence still for? Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser and Polosukhin answered in 2017 with "Attention Is All You Need": nothing. Delete the recurrence, keep the attention, add some feed-forward layers and normalization, and you get a model that is easier to parallelize on GPUs, easier to optimize at depth, and that scales to sizes no recurrent model ever reached.

The Transformer is now the default architecture for language, and has become dominant in vision (Week 11), speech, protein modeling and more. This week is therefore the pivot of the course. We build it piece by piece, from first principles, and we are pedantic about shapes because most real-world Transformer bugs are shape or masking bugs. Week 10 then asks what happens when you pretrain this architecture on a large fraction of the internet.

A mental model to carry through the week

A Transformer layer is two operations alternated: communication (attention: tokens exchange information, a weighted average over positions) and computation (the feed-forward network: each token is transformed independently). Residual connections form a "highway" (the residual stream) that every sublayer reads from and writes to. Nearly everything in this chapter is a detail about one of those three ideas.

From recurrence to attention-only models

Recurrent networks have two structural problems, both visible in Week 7. First, they are sequential: the hidden state ht\boldsymbol{h}_tht​ needs ht−1\boldsymbol{h}_{t-1}ht−1​, so a sequence of length nnn requires nnn dependent steps and a GPU sits mostly idle. Second, information from step iii to step jjj must pass through ∣i−j∣|i-j|∣i−j∣ nonlinear transformations, so long-range dependencies are hard to learn even with gating. Convolutional sequence models (Week 7) shorten that path to O(log⁡kn)O(\log_k n)O(logk​n) with dilation, but still not to one.

Self-attention has a path length of exactly one between any pair of positions, and all positions are computed in parallel. The price is that it costs O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) time and memory in the sequence length, and that it is blind to order unless we inject position information separately. Both costs are real and shape most of this week.

Layer type Sequential ops Max path length Cost per layer
Recurrent O(n)O(n)O(n) O(n)O(n)O(n) O(nd2)O(n d^2)O(nd2)
Convolutional (kernel kkk) O(1)O(1)O(1) O(log⁡kn)O(\log_k n)O(logk​n) with dilation O(knd2)O(k n d^2)O(knd2)
Self-attention O(1)O(1)O(1) O(1)O(1)O(1) O(n2d+nd2)O(n^2 d + n d^2)O(n2d+nd2)
Where the pieces came from

Attention in neural translation is due to Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2014/2015) and Luong et al. (2015). Self-attention (a sequence attending to itself) appeared in Cheng et al. (2016), Parikh et al. (2016) and Lin et al. (2017), usually inside recurrent models. The 2017 paper combined self-attention with residual connections (He et al. 2016), layer normalization (Ba, Kiros and Hinton, 2016), multi-head projections and sinusoidal position signals, and trained it for translation in a few days on eight GPUs, beating the best recurrent and convolutional systems. The architecture was subsequently reused almost unchanged for GPT (2018), BERT (2018) and everything since.

Self-attention from first principles

Attention as a soft dictionary lookup

Start with something familiar: a Python dictionary. A lookup d[query] compares the query against each stored key; if one key matches exactly, it returns that key's value. This is hard, all-or-nothing retrieval.

Now make it soft. Suppose keys and queries are vectors, and "match" means a high dot product. Instead of returning one value, return a weighted average of all values, where the weights are larger for keys that match the query better. Weights must be non-negative and sum to one, which is exactly what the softmax produces:

attend(q;{(kj,vj)}j=1n)  =  ∑j=1nαjvj,αj=exp⁡(q⊤kj)∑lexp⁡(q⊤kl).\text{attend}(\boldsymbol{q}; \{(\boldsymbol{k}_j, \boldsymbol{v}_j)\}_{j=1}^n) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_j \boldsymbol{v}_j, \qquad \alpha_j = \frac{\exp(\boldsymbol{q}^\top \boldsymbol{k}_j)}{\sum_{l}\exp(\boldsymbol{q}^\top \boldsymbol{k}_l)}.attend(q;{(kj​,vj​)}j=1n​)=j=1∑n​αj​vj​,αj​=∑l​exp(q⊤kl​)exp(q⊤kj​)​.

That is the whole mechanism. When the query matches one key much better than the others, α\alphaα is nearly one-hot and the result is nearly a hard lookup. When the query matches many keys similarly, the result is an average. The three roles are worth naming precisely:

  • the query says "what am I looking for?"
  • the key says "what do I contain, as far as matching is concerned?"
  • the value says "what will I contribute if I am selected?"

Where Q, K and V come from

In self-attention, queries, keys and values are all computed from the same sequence of token representations. Let X∈Rn×d\mathbf{X}\in\R^{n\times d}X∈Rn×d be the matrix whose row iii is the vector xi\boldsymbol{x}_ixi​ of token iii (nnn tokens, model width d=dmodeld = d_\text{model}d=dmodel​). Three learned linear maps produce the three roles:

Q=XWQ,K=XWK,V=XWV,\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_Q,\qquad \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_K,\qquad \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_V,Q=XWQ​,K=XWK​,V=XWV​,

with WQ,WK∈Rd×dk\mathbf{W}_Q,\mathbf{W}_K\in\R^{d\times d_k}WQ​,WK​∈Rd×dk​ and WV∈Rd×dv\mathbf{W}_V\in\R^{d\times d_v}WV​∈Rd×dv​. Why three different projections of the same input rather than using xi\boldsymbol{x}_ixi​ directly? Because the three jobs differ. In the sentence "the animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired", the word "it" should look for a noun-like thing (a query feature), the word "animal" should advertise that it is a noun and an animate subject (a key feature), and what "animal" passes along once selected (the value) may be a different set of features again. Separate projections let the model decouple matching from content. In an RNN the single hidden state had to serve all roles at once.

Scaled dot-product attention

Stacking all nnn queries gives the matrix form used everywhere:

Attention(Q,K,V)  =  softmax⁡ ⁣(QK⊤dk)V.\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V}) \;=\; \softmax\!\Big(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)\mathbf{V}.Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤​)V.

The shapes are: QK⊤∈Rn×n\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top\in\R^{n\times n}QK⊤∈Rn×n (entry (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) is the score between query iii and key jjj), the softmax is applied along each row (over keys), and multiplying by V∈Rn×dv\mathbf{V}\in\R^{n\times d_v}V∈Rn×dv​ yields Rn×dv\R^{n\times d_v}Rn×dv​: one output vector per token. Write the output for token iii explicitly:

oi=∑j=1nαij vj,αij=exp⁡(qi⊤kj/dk)∑l=1nexp⁡(qi⊤kl/dk).\boldsymbol{o}_i = \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_{ij}\,\boldsymbol{v}_j,\qquad \alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp\big(\boldsymbol{q}_i^\top\boldsymbol{k}_j/\sqrt{d_k}\big)}{\sum_{l=1}^n \exp\big(\boldsymbol{q}_i^\top\boldsymbol{k}_l/\sqrt{d_k}\big)}.oi​=j=1∑n​αij​vj​,αij​=∑l=1n​exp(qi⊤​kl​/dk​​)exp(qi⊤​kj​/dk​​)​.

Two properties are worth internalizing right away.

  1. Each output is a convex combination of value vectors. Attention can only route and average existing information; non-linear processing happens elsewhere (the feed-forward layer).
  2. Self-attention is permutation-equivariant. If you shuffle the rows of X\mathbf{X}X, the rows of the output are shuffled the same way and are otherwise unchanged. The layer has no idea which token came first. This is why position must be injected explicitly (see Positional information).
Proof of permutation equivariance

Let P\mathbf{P}P be a permutation matrix. Then Q′=PXWQ=PQ\mathbf{Q}' = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_Q = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{Q}Q′=PXWQ​=PQ, and likewise K′=PK\mathbf{K}'=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{K}K′=PK, V′=PV\mathbf{V}'=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}V′=PV. The score matrix becomes PQK⊤P⊤\mathbf{P}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top\mathbf{P}^\topPQK⊤P⊤, and a row-wise softmax commutes with simultaneous row and column permutation, so the weights are PAP⊤\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}^\topPAP⊤. The output is PAP⊤PV=PAV\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}^\top\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}PAP⊤PV=PAV, using P⊤P=I\mathbf{P}^\top\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{I}P⊤P=I. So permuting the input permutes the output. ■\blacksquare■

A single attention head in NumPy

Before PyTorch, the whole mechanism fits in a dozen lines. Read the shapes in the comments.

pythonattention_numpy.py
import numpy as np

def softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = z - z.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)      # subtract max for numerical stability
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

def attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, causal=False):
    """X: (n, d). Wq, Wk: (d, d_k). Wv: (d, d_v). Returns (out (n, d_v), A (n, n))."""
    Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv             # (n, d_k), (n, d_k), (n, d_v)
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(Q.shape[-1])            # (n, n) scaled scores
    if causal:                                    # forbid attending to the future
        S = np.where(np.triu(np.ones_like(S), k=1) == 1, -np.inf, S)
    A = softmax(S, axis=-1)                       # (n, n); every row sums to 1
    return A @ V, A                               # (n, d_v)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d, dk = 5, 16, 8
X = rng.standard_normal((n, d))
Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.standard_normal((d, dk)) / np.sqrt(d) for _ in range(3))
out, A = attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, causal=True)
print(out.shape, A.shape)                         # (5, 8) (5, 5)
print(np.round(A, 2))                             # lower-triangular rows summing to 1

# permutation equivariance check (non-causal): permuting inputs permutes outputs
perm = rng.permutation(n)
out_a, _ = attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv)
out_b, _ = attention(X[perm], Wq, Wk, Wv)
print(np.allclose(out_a[perm], out_b))            # True

Why divide by the square root of the key dimension

The factor 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_k}1/dk​​ looks like a cosmetic constant. It is not. It is what keeps the softmax usable as dkd_kdk​ grows, and the argument is a short variance computation.

Treat a query and a key as random vectors with independent components of mean 0 and variance 1 (this is roughly what a well-initialized network produces, cf. Week 3). The score is s=q⊤k=∑m=1dkqmkms = \boldsymbol{q}^\top\boldsymbol{k} = \sum_{m=1}^{d_k} q_m k_ms=q⊤k=∑m=1dk​​qm​km​.

Variance of the dot product

Each product qmkmq_mk_mqm​km​ has mean E[qm]E[km]=0\E[q_m]\E[k_m]=0E[qm​]E[km​]=0 and, by independence, variance E[qm2]E[km2]=1⋅1=1\E[q_m^2]\E[k_m^2] = 1\cdot 1 = 1E[qm2​]E[km2​]=1⋅1=1. The dkd_kdk​ terms are independent, so variances add:

E[s]=0,Var⁡(s)=dk.\E[s] = 0,\qquad \Var(s) = d_k.E[s]=0,Var(s)=dk​.

The standard deviation is dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​. Dividing by dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ gives Var⁡(s/dk)=1\Var(s/\sqrt{d_k}) = 1Var(s/dk​​)=1 for every dkd_kdk​. ■\blacksquare■

Why does the size of the logits matter? Consider the softmax αj∝esj\alpha_j\propto e^{s_j}αj​∝esj​. If the logits have standard deviation σ\sigmaσ, then the gap between the largest and the typical logit is about σ\sigmaσ times a number of order one (growing slowly with the number of keys). With σ=1\sigma=1σ=1 the largest weight is moderate. With σ=dk=8\sigma=\sqrt{d_k}=8σ=dk​​=8 (as in dk=64d_k=64dk​=64) the largest logit dominates by factors like e8≈3000e^{8}\approx 3000e8≈3000, and the softmax output is nearly one-hot.

That is a problem for learning, not only for expressiveness. The softmax Jacobian is

∂αi∂sj=αi(δij−αj),\frac{\partial \alpha_i}{\partial s_j} = \alpha_i(\delta_{ij}-\alpha_j),∂sj​∂αi​​=αi​(δij​−αj​),

and when α\boldsymbol{\alpha}α is nearly one-hot, every entry is close to zero (αi≈1\alpha_i\approx1αi​≈1 gives αi(1−αi)≈0\alpha_i(1-\alpha_i)\approx 0αi​(1−αi​)≈0; αi≈0\alpha_i\approx 0αi​≈0 gives a tiny product). The gradient flowing back to WQ\mathbf{W}_QWQ​ and WK\mathbf{W}_KWK​ vanishes, the heads freeze into arbitrary hard patterns early in training, and optimization stalls. You can see both effects in real numbers:

The second chart is the important one. With 16 random keys, a uniform softmax would put 0.0625 on each; unscaled logits at dk=1024d_k=1024dk​=1024 give the largest key an average weight of 0.96, while scaled logits stay at about 0.25 regardless of dkd_kdk​. (Vaswani et al. note the same effect; additive attention was reported to beat unscaled dot-product attention at large dkd_kdk​ for this reason.)

Scaling is about the *initial* distribution, not a law

Once the model trains, the logits are no longer unit-variance, and that is fine: a sharp, nearly one-hot head is sometimes exactly what is needed. The 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_k}1/dk​​ factor merely guarantees a healthy starting point. Some recent models add extra stabilizers such as QK-norm (normalizing queries and keys before the dot product) because logits can still grow uncontrollably at large scale, a failure sometimes called attention-logit growth or entropy collapse.

Temperature and the geometry of attention

The 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_k}1/dk​​ is a fixed temperature. If you write α=softmax⁡(s/τ)\alpha = \softmax(\mathbf{s}/\tau)α=softmax(s/τ), then τ→∞\tau\to\inftyτ→∞ gives uniform averaging, τ→0\tau\to0τ→0 gives hard argmax retrieval, and standard attention sits at τ=dk\tau=\sqrt{d_k}τ=dk​​ for raw scores. The explorer above exposes τ\tauτ so you can see the interpolation: row entropy goes from log⁡n\log nlogn (uniform) to 000 (one-hot). Keep this picture; in Week 10 the same knob appears again when we sample text.

Multi-head attention

One attention head produces one weighted average per token. But a token typically needs several different kinds of information at once: the previous token, the syntactic head, a coreferent noun, a matching bracket. A single softmax has to compromise. Multi-head attention runs hhh attention operations in parallel in lower-dimensional subspaces and concatenates the results.

Definition and the shape bookkeeping

Let ddd be the model width and hhh the number of heads, with dk=dv=d/hd_k = d_v = d/hdk​=dv​=d/h. For head r∈{1,…,h}r\in\{1,\dots,h\}r∈{1,…,h}:

headr=Attention(XWQ(r),  XWK(r),  XWV(r)),MHA(X)=[head1;… ;headh]WO,\text{head}_r = \text{Attention}\big(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_Q^{(r)},\;\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_K^{(r)},\;\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_V^{(r)}\big),\qquad \text{MHA}(\mathbf{X}) = \big[\text{head}_1;\dots;\text{head}_h\big]\mathbf{W}_O,headr​=Attention(XWQ(r)​,XWK(r)​,XWV(r)​),MHA(X)=[head1​;…;headh​]WO​,

where WQ(r),WK(r),WV(r)∈Rd×d/h\mathbf{W}_Q^{(r)},\mathbf{W}_K^{(r)},\mathbf{W}_V^{(r)}\in\R^{d\times d/h}WQ(r)​,WK(r)​,WV(r)​∈Rd×d/h and WO∈Rd×d\mathbf{W}_O\in\R^{d\times d}WO​∈Rd×d. The cost is the same as one big head: hhh matrices of shape d×(d/h)d\times (d/h)d×(d/h) hold the same number of weights as one d×dd\times dd×d matrix. In practice one fuses them: compute XWQ\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_QXWQ​ with a single d×dd\times dd×d matrix and then reshape the result into hhh heads. Here are the exact tensor shapes with a batch dimension BBB, sequence length TTT:

Step Operation Shape
input X\mathbf{X}X (B, T, d)
project X @ W_Q (also K, V) (B, T, d)
split heads view(B, T, h, d_k) then transpose(1, 2) (B, h, T, d_k)
scores Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / sqrt(d_k) (B, h, T, T)
weights softmax(dim=-1) (B, h, T, T)
weighted values A @ V (B, h, T, d_k)
merge heads transpose(1, 2) then reshape(B, T, d) (B, T, d)
output projection @ W_O (B, T, d)

The output has the same shape as the input, which is what lets us stack layers and add residual connections.

Why subspaces rather than hhh full-width heads?

If every head used the full width ddd, cost would grow hhh-fold. Splitting ddd into hhh slices of width d/hd/hd/h keeps the budget constant while giving each head its own softmax, hence its own attention pattern. The trade-off is that each head's queries and keys live in a smaller space, which limits how many independent "match features" it can express. Empirically dkd_kdk​ between 64 and 128 is the sweet spot, and most models scale heads with width (d=768,h=12d=768, h=12d=768,h=12; d=12288,h=96d=12288, h=96d=12288,h=96 gives dk=128d_k=128dk​=128).

What do heads learn?

Studies of trained models (Voita et al., 2019, on translation; Clark et al., 2019, on BERT; Olsson et al., 2022, "induction heads" in GPT-style models) find that heads specialize: some attend to the previous token, some to rare or syntactically salient tokens, some implement a copy-and-continue pattern ("... A B ... A" predicts "B") that appears to underlie in-context learning. Many heads can also be pruned with little loss, which tells you that head count is partly redundancy. Treat attention weights as a useful diagnostic, not a faithful explanation of the model's reasoning: a high weight does not guarantee a high influence on the output, because the value vector's norm and what later layers do with it also matter.

Multi-head attention in PyTorch

This is a complete, mask-aware implementation. It uses torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention when you want speed (it dispatches to fused FlashAttention-style kernels on supported GPUs), and an explicit path so you can see the math and inspect the weights.

pythonmha.py
import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model: int, n_heads: int, dropout: float = 0.0, bias: bool = True):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0, "d_model must be divisible by n_heads"
        self.h, self.dk = n_heads, d_model // n_heads
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model, bias=bias)    # fused W_Q, W_K, W_V
        self.out = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=bias)         # W_O
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, x, mask=None, return_weights=False):
        """x: (B, T, d). mask: bool broadcastable to (B, h, T, T), True = may attend."""
        B, T, d = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).split(d, dim=-1)                    # each (B, T, d)
        # (B, T, d) -> (B, T, h, dk) -> (B, h, T, dk)
        q, k, v = (t.view(B, T, self.h, self.dk).transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v))
        if return_weights:                                        # explicit path
            s = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(self.dk)      # (B, h, T, T)
            if mask is not None:
                s = s.masked_fill(~mask, float("-inf"))
            a = self.drop(torch.softmax(s, dim=-1))
            y = a @ v                                             # (B, h, T, dk)
        else:                                                     # fused kernel path
            y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=mask,
                                               dropout_p=self.drop.p if self.training else 0.0)
            a = None
        y = y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, d)                    # merge heads -> (B, T, d)
        y = self.out(y)
        return (y, a) if return_weights else y

if __name__ == "__main__":
    B, T, d, h = 2, 6, 64, 8
    x = torch.randn(B, T, d)
    causal = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool))       # (T, T), True on/below diagonal
    mha = MultiHeadAttention(d, h)
    y, a = mha(x, mask=causal, return_weights=True)
    print(y.shape, a.shape)                                       # (2, 6, 64) (2, 8, 6, 6)
    print(a[0, 0].sum(-1))                                        # each row sums to 1
    print((a[0, 0].triu(1) == 0).all())                           # no weight on the future
    y2 = mha(x, mask=causal)                                      # fused path agrees
    print(torch.allclose(y, y2, atol=1e-5))

Notice that scaled_dot_product_attention interprets a boolean mask with True meaning "take part in attention", whereas a float mask is added to the scores. Mixing the two conventions is a classic bug (see Common mistakes).

Cross-attention

In the original encoder-decoder Transformer a third attention type appears: cross-attention. Its queries come from the decoder's states and its keys and values from the encoder's output ("memory"). Everything else is identical, except that the score matrix is Tdec×TencT_\text{dec}\times T_\text{enc}Tdec​×Tenc​ rather than square. This is the direct descendant of Bahdanau attention from Week 7: the decoder looks at the source sentence while generating each target word.

The position-wise feed-forward network

After attention mixes information across positions, each token passes independently through the same two-layer MLP:

FFN(x)=W2 ϕ(W1x+b1)+b2,W1∈Rdff×d, W2∈Rd×dff,\text{FFN}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \mathbf{W}_2\,\phi(\mathbf{W}_1\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{b}_1) + \boldsymbol{b}_2,\qquad \mathbf{W}_1\in\R^{d_\text{ff}\times d},\ \mathbf{W}_2\in\R^{d\times d_\text{ff}},FFN(x)=W2​ϕ(W1​x+b1​)+b2​,W1​∈Rdff​×d, W2​∈Rd×dff​,

with dff=4dd_\text{ff}=4ddff​=4d by convention (2048 for d=512d=512d=512 in the original paper) and ϕ\phiϕ originally ReLU, later GELU (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016) in BERT and GPT. "Position-wise" means the same weights are applied to every position; it is equivalent to two 1×11\times11×1 convolutions.

Why do we need it?

Without the FFN a stack of attention layers is surprisingly weak. Each attention output is a convex combination of linearly projected inputs; stacking just re-mixes linear functions of the token embeddings through input-dependent weights. The FFN supplies the element-wise non-linearity and the bulk of the capacity: it holds about two thirds of the parameters of a block (8d28d^28d2 versus 4d24d^24d2 for attention, derived below).

A useful reading, from Geva, Schuster, Berant and Levy (2021), treats the FFN as a key-value memory: the rows of W1\mathbf{W}_1W1​ act as keys that detect patterns in the residual stream, and the columns of W2\mathbf{W}_2W2​ are the values written back when the corresponding hidden unit fires. Attention then moves information between tokens, and the FFN looks facts up within a token. This division (communication versus computation) is a good heuristic for where to look when you study what a model "knows".

Gated variants: GLU, SwiGLU

Shazeer (2020, "GLU Variants Improve Transformer") showed that replacing the first linear layer and activation by a gated product gives consistently lower loss at the same compute:

FFNSwiGLU(x)=W2(SiLU(Wgx)⊙(Wux)),\text{FFN}_\text{SwiGLU}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \mathbf{W}_2\big(\text{SiLU}(\mathbf{W}_g\boldsymbol{x})\odot(\mathbf{W}_u\boldsymbol{x})\big),FFNSwiGLU​(x)=W2​(SiLU(Wg​x)⊙(Wu​x)),

where SiLU(z)=z σ(z)\text{SiLU}(z)=z\,\sigma(z)SiLU(z)=zσ(z) and ⊙\odot⊙ is element-wise multiplication. There are now three matrices instead of two, so to keep the parameter count equal models shrink the hidden width to roughly 83d\tfrac{8}{3}d38​d (rounded to a hardware-friendly multiple). LLaMA-family and many other open models use this form. The gate lets each hidden unit decide how much of its input to pass, a mild form of multiplicative interaction.

pythonffn.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class FFN(nn.Module):                       # GPT-2 style
    def __init__(self, d, mult=4, dropout=0.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.w1, self.w2 = nn.Linear(d, mult * d), nn.Linear(mult * d, d)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout)
    def forward(self, x):                   # (B, T, d) -> (B, T, d)
        return self.drop(self.w2(F.gelu(self.w1(x))))

class SwiGLU(nn.Module):                    # LLaMA style, no biases
    def __init__(self, d, hidden=None):
        super().__init__()
        hidden = hidden or int(8 * d / 3)
        self.gate, self.up, self.down = (nn.Linear(d, hidden, bias=False),
                                         nn.Linear(d, hidden, bias=False),
                                         nn.Linear(hidden, d, bias=False))
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.down(F.silu(self.gate(x)) * self.up(x))

d = 512
n1 = sum(p.numel() for p in FFN(d).parameters())
n2 = sum(p.numel() for p in SwiGLU(d).parameters())
print(n1, n2)    # 2099712 vs 2096640: hidden = int(8d/3) = 1365 matches the 4x GELU FFN to within 0.2%
Mixture of experts in one paragraph

Because the FFN holds most parameters and processes tokens independently, it is the natural place to add capacity cheaply. A mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer replaces one FFN by many (say 8 to 64), plus a small router that sends each token to its top-1 or top-2 experts (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus, Zoph and Shazeer, 2021, "Switch Transformer"). Parameters grow by the number of experts while per-token FLOPs stay about constant. The cost is memory, load-balancing losses and communication.

Residual connections and normalization

The residual stream

Each sublayer (attention or FFN) is wrapped in a residual connection: the output is x+Sublayer(x)\boldsymbol{x} + \text{Sublayer}(\boldsymbol{x})x+Sublayer(x), as in ResNets (Week 6). In a Transformer this has a particularly clean interpretation due to Elhage et al. (2021): the vector at each position is a residual stream, a running sum to which every attention head and every FFN adds its contribution. Layer ℓ\ellℓ reads from the stream (through a projection), computes something, and writes the result back by addition. Nothing is ever overwritten; information from the embedding can flow unchanged to the last layer.

That has an optimization benefit identical to ResNets (the gradient of the loss with respect to an early layer contains a direct identity path), and a conceptual one: a 96-layer model is not a 96-step bottleneck but a shared workspace that layers incrementally edit.

Layer normalization

Batch normalization (Week 3) is awkward for sequences: batch statistics are noisy with variable lengths and padding, and in autoregressive decoding the batch may be a single sequence. Layer normalization (Ba, Kiros and Hinton, 2016) normalizes each token vector over its feature dimension, independently of the batch and of the other positions:

LN(x)=γ⊙x−μσ2+ϵ+β,μ=1d∑mxm,σ2=1d∑m(xm−μ)2,\text{LN}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{\gamma}\odot\frac{\boldsymbol{x}-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}} + \boldsymbol{\beta},\qquad \mu=\frac1d\sum_{m}x_m,\quad \sigma^2 = \frac1d\sum_m (x_m-\mu)^2,LN(x)=γ⊙σ2+ϵ​x−μ​+β,μ=d1​m∑​xm​,σ2=d1​m∑​(xm​−μ)2,

with learned gain γ\boldsymbol{\gamma}γ and bias β\boldsymbol{\beta}β in Rd\R^dRd and ϵ≈10−5\epsilon\approx10^{-5}ϵ≈10−5 for numerical safety. In PyTorch, nn.LayerNorm(d) normalizes over the last dimension: the statistics are computed per token, so (B, T, d) produces B⋅TB\cdot TB⋅T separate means and variances.

RMSNorm

Zhang and Sennrich (2019) observed that re-centering (subtracting μ\muμ) contributes little and that the benefit of LayerNorm comes mostly from re-scaling. RMSNorm drops the mean and the bias:

RMSNorm(x)=γ⊙x1d∑mxm2+ϵ.\text{RMSNorm}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{\gamma}\odot\frac{\boldsymbol{x}}{\sqrt{\tfrac1d\sum_m x_m^2+\epsilon}}.RMSNorm(x)=γ⊙d1​∑m​xm2​+ϵ​x​.

It is cheaper (one reduction instead of two, no bias) and works as well in practice; LLaMA, Mistral, Gemma and many others use it. Both normalizations are scale-invariant in their input: multiplying x\boldsymbol{x}x by a positive constant leaves the output unchanged, which is a useful fact when thinking about what the residual stream's norm means.

pythonnorms.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, eps=1e-6):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d))       # gamma
    def forward(self, x):                                # x: (..., d)
        # compute in float32 for stability even if x is bf16/fp16, then cast back
        xf = x.float()
        out = xf * torch.rsqrt(xf.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)
        return (out.type_as(x)) * self.weight

x = torch.randn(4, 10, 64) * 5 + 3
ln, rms = nn.LayerNorm(64), RMSNorm(64)
print(ln(x).mean(-1).abs().max().item())                 # ~0: LN removes the per-token mean
print(rms(x).mean(-1).abs().max().item())                # not 0: RMSNorm keeps the mean
print(rms(x).pow(2).mean(-1).sqrt().mean().item())       # ~1: unit RMS per token

Pre-norm versus post-norm

Where does the normalization go? The original Transformer used post-norm: apply the sublayer, add the residual, then normalize, x←LN(x+Sublayer(x))\boldsymbol{x}\leftarrow\text{LN}(\boldsymbol{x}+\text{Sublayer}(\boldsymbol{x}))x←LN(x+Sublayer(x)). GPT-2 and nearly every large model since use pre-norm: normalize first, x←x+Sublayer(LN(x))\boldsymbol{x}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{x}+\text{Sublayer}(\text{LN}(\boldsymbol{x}))x←x+Sublayer(LN(x)), with one extra final LayerNorm before the output head.

The difference is about gradient flow. In post-norm, every residual addition is followed by a normalization, so the identity path is interrupted 2N2N2N times in an NNN-layer model, and gradient magnitudes at initialization are largest for the last layers (Xiong et al., 2020 analyze this for post-norm at initialization). The consequence is that post-norm models need a careful learning-rate warmup or they diverge; with pre-norm the gradient scale is roughly uniform across depth, training is stable with little or no warmup and larger learning rates, and 100-layer-plus models train reliably.

A one-line view of the residual stream under pre-norm

Unrolling xℓ+1=xℓ+Fℓ(LN(xℓ))\boldsymbol{x}_{\ell+1}=\boldsymbol{x}_\ell+F_\ell(\text{LN}(\boldsymbol{x}_\ell))xℓ+1​=xℓ​+Fℓ​(LN(xℓ​)) gives xL=x0+∑ℓ=0L−1Fℓ(LN(xℓ)),\boldsymbol{x}_L = \boldsymbol{x}_0 + \sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1} F_\ell(\text{LN}(\boldsymbol{x}_\ell)),xL​=x0​+ℓ=0∑L−1​Fℓ​(LN(xℓ​)), so ∂xL/∂x0=I+(terms from the Fℓ)\partial\boldsymbol{x}_L/\partial\boldsymbol{x}_0 = \mathbf{I}+(\text{terms from the }F_\ell)∂xL​/∂x0​=I+(terms from the Fℓ​) always contains an identity term. Under post-norm each step applies a normalization to the whole sum, and no such clean expansion exists.

The cost of pre-norm: the residual stream's norm grows with depth (each layer adds to it), so later layers' contributions are relatively smaller, and some experiments find post-norm reaches slightly better final quality when it can be made to train (DeepNorm, Wang et al. 2022, is a modified post-norm that trains 1000-layer models). The practical rule: use pre-norm (with RMSNorm) unless you have a reason not to, and always add the final norm.

Positional information

Since self-attention is permutation-equivariant, a model fed only token embeddings sees a bag of words. We must tell it where each token is. There are two broad strategies:

  • Absolute schemes add (or concatenate) a vector that depends on the position ppp to the token embedding, once, at the input.
  • Relative schemes change the attention score so it depends on the offset n−mn-mn−m between query position mmm and key position nnn, applied in every layer.

Which is better is an empirical question that the field answered gradually in favor of relative schemes, especially RoPE. We cover each, with the derivations that explain their properties.

Sinusoidal encodings

The original paper used fixed (not learned) vectors PE(p)∈Rd\text{PE}(p)\in\R^dPE(p)∈Rd, with pairs of coordinates oscillating at geometrically spaced frequencies:

PE(p)2i=sin⁡(p ωi),PE(p)2i+1=cos⁡(p ωi),ωi=10000−2i/d,i=0,…,d/2−1.\text{PE}(p)_{2i} = \sin(p\,\omega_i),\quad \text{PE}(p)_{2i+1} = \cos(p\,\omega_i),\qquad \omega_i = 10000^{-2i/d},\quad i=0,\dots,d/2-1.PE(p)2i​=sin(pωi​),PE(p)2i+1​=cos(pωi​),ωi​=10000−2i/d,i=0,…,d/2−1.

Think of it as a bank of clocks: pair 0 ticks fast (wavelength 2π≈6.32\pi\approx6.32π≈6.3 positions), the last pair ticks very slowly (wavelength about 2π⋅100002\pi\cdot100002π⋅10000). Reading all the clocks together identifies a position uniquely, like reading seconds, minutes and hours; and like a binary counter the low-order bits flip fast and the high-order bits slowly.

The encoding is added to the token embedding: xp=Emb(wp)+PE(p)\boldsymbol{x}_p = \text{Emb}(w_p)+\text{PE}(p)xp​=Emb(wp​)+PE(p). Try the visualizer; the left columns of the matrix oscillate quickly, the right ones slowly.

InteractivePosition encodings: matrix, offset similarity, RoPE and ALiBi
Why sinusoids: shifts are linear maps, and dot products depend on the offset

Fix a frequency ω\omegaω. Write the pair at position ppp as up=(sin⁡pω,cos⁡pω)⊤\boldsymbol{u}_p=(\sin p\omega,\cos p\omega)^\topup​=(sinpω,cospω)⊤. The angle-addition formulas give

(sin⁡(p+k)ωcos⁡(p+k)ω)=(cos⁡kωsin⁡kω−sin⁡kωcos⁡kω)(sin⁡pωcos⁡pω).\begin{pmatrix}\sin (p+k)\omega\\ \cos (p+k)\omega\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos k\omega & \sin k\omega\\ -\sin k\omega & \cos k\omega\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}\sin p\omega\\ \cos p\omega\end{pmatrix}.(sin(p+k)ωcos(p+k)ω​)=(coskω−sinkω​sinkωcoskω​)(sinpωcospω​).

So up+k=Mkup\boldsymbol{u}_{p+k}=\mathbf{M}_k\boldsymbol{u}_pup+k​=Mk​up​, where the matrix Mk\mathbf{M}_kMk​ (a rotation by −kω-k\omega−kω in this coordinate order) depends on the offset kkk only, not on ppp. Hence for any fixed kkk, PE(p+k)\text{PE}(p+k)PE(p+k) is a linear function of PE(p)\text{PE}(p)PE(p), which a linear layer could in principle exploit to attend by offset. Moreover the dot product of two encodings is

PE(p)⊤PE(p+k)=∑i[sin⁡pωisin⁡(p+k)ωi+cos⁡pωicos⁡(p+k)ωi]=∑i=0d/2−1cos⁡(k ωi),\text{PE}(p)^\top\text{PE}(p+k)=\sum_{i}\big[\sin p\omega_i\sin (p+k)\omega_i+\cos p\omega_i\cos(p+k)\omega_i\big]=\sum_{i=0}^{d/2-1}\cos(k\,\omega_i),PE(p)⊤PE(p+k)=i∑​[sinpωi​sin(p+k)ωi​+cospωi​cos(p+k)ωi​]=i=0∑d/2−1​cos(kωi​),

using cos⁡(a−b)=cos⁡acos⁡b+sin⁡asin⁡b\cos(a-b)=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin bcos(a−b)=cosacosb+sinasinb. It depends only on the offset kkk, is symmetric in kkk, and decays as ∣k∣|k|∣k∣ grows. ■\blacksquare■

The chart shows this numerically for d=128d=128d=128. Note an important limitation: the dot product above is between inputs. After the learned projections WQ,WK\mathbf{W}_Q,\mathbf{W}_KWQ​,WK​ and after many layers the clean "function of offset only" property is no longer guaranteed, which is one motivation for relative schemes that build it into the score itself.

pythonsinusoidal.py
import math, torch

def sinusoidal_pe(T: int, d: int, base: float = 10000.0) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Returns (T, d). Even columns sin, odd columns cos (interleaved, as in the paper)."""
    pos = torch.arange(T, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None]                    # (T, 1)
    inv = torch.exp(-math.log(base) * torch.arange(0, d, 2).float() / d)   # (d/2,) = base^(-2i/d)
    pe = torch.zeros(T, d)
    pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(pos * inv)
    pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(pos * inv)
    return pe

pe = sinusoidal_pe(100, 128)
print(pe.shape)                                    # torch.Size([100, 128])
# dot product depends only on the offset: compare (10, 15) with (60, 65)
print(torch.allclose(pe[10] @ pe[15], pe[60] @ pe[65], atol=1e-3))   # True

Learned absolute embeddings

BERT and GPT-2 instead learn a table nn.Embedding(max_len, d) and add the row for position ppp. It is the simplest possible scheme and works as well as sinusoids within the training length (the original paper reports near-identical translation quality). Its limits: positions beyond max_len do not exist, and the table cannot generalize to unseen lengths (a position never seen in training has an untrained embedding). It also spends Tmax⋅dT_\text{max}\cdot dTmax​⋅d parameters (0.8M for GPT-2 small, small next to 124M).

Relative position representations

Intuition says language is mostly about relative position: the previous word, the word three back. Shaw, Uszkoreit and Vaswani (2018) modified attention so the score and the value aggregation both receive a learned vector an−mK,an−mV\boldsymbol{a}^K_{n-m},\boldsymbol{a}^V_{n-m}an−mK​,an−mV​ indexed by the clipped offset. Transformer-XL (Dai et al., 2019) reparameterized the score into content-content, content-position, global-content-bias and global-position-bias terms so that attention could span recurrently cached segments. T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) used the simplest form: a learned scalar bias per head added to the logit, indexed by a bucketed offset b(n−m)b(n-m)b(n−m) (exact buckets for small offsets, logarithmically larger buckets for distant ones):

smn=qm⊤kndk+b b(n−m)(head).s_{mn} = \frac{\boldsymbol{q}_m^\top\boldsymbol{k}_n}{\sqrt{d_k}} + b^{(\text{head})}_{\,b(n-m)}.smn​=dk​​qm⊤​kn​​+bb(n−m)(head)​.

This is cheap (a small table per head) and extends to longer sequences by sharing the last bucket. The downside is that the bias must be materialized as an n×nn\times nn×n addition to the scores, which complicates fused attention kernels.

Rotary position embeddings (RoPE)

RoFormer (Su, Lu, Pan, Murtadha, Wen and Liu, 2021) introduced rotary embeddings, which are now the default in LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and many other open models. The idea: rotate the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their position, so that the dot product between a rotated query and a rotated key depends only on the angle difference, hence on the relative offset.

Deriving RoPE

We want functions fq(x,m)f_q(\boldsymbol{x},m)fq​(x,m) and fk(x,n)f_k(\boldsymbol{x},n)fk​(x,n) that inject positions m,nm,nm,n such that the score depends only on q,k\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{k}q,k and n−mn-mn−m: ⟨fq(q,m), fk(k,n)⟩=g(q,k,n−m).\langle f_q(\boldsymbol{q},m),\,f_k(\boldsymbol{k},n)\rangle = g(\boldsymbol{q},\boldsymbol{k},n-m).⟨fq​(q,m),fk​(k,n)⟩=g(q,k,n−m). Work in two dimensions first. Let R(ϕ)=(cos⁡ϕ−sin⁡ϕsin⁡ϕcos⁡ϕ)\mathbf{R}(\phi)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\phi&-\sin\phi\\ \sin\phi&\cos\phi\end{pmatrix}R(ϕ)=(cosϕsinϕ​−sinϕcosϕ​) be a rotation. Rotations are orthogonal, R(ϕ)⊤=R(−ϕ)\mathbf{R}(\phi)^\top=\mathbf{R}(-\phi)R(ϕ)⊤=R(−ϕ), and compose by adding angles, R(a)R(b)=R(a+b)\mathbf{R}(a)\mathbf{R}(b)=\mathbf{R}(a+b)R(a)R(b)=R(a+b). Choose fq(q,m)=R(mθ)q,fk(k,n)=R(nθ)k.f_q(\boldsymbol{q},m)=\mathbf{R}(m\theta)\boldsymbol{q},\qquad f_k(\boldsymbol{k},n)=\mathbf{R}(n\theta)\boldsymbol{k}.fq​(q,m)=R(mθ)q,fk​(k,n)=R(nθ)k. Then (R(mθ)q)⊤(R(nθ)k)=q⊤R(−mθ)R(nθ)k=q⊤R((n−m)θ)k.\big(\mathbf{R}(m\theta)\boldsymbol{q}\big)^\top\big(\mathbf{R}(n\theta)\boldsymbol{k}\big)=\boldsymbol{q}^\top\mathbf{R}(-m\theta)\mathbf{R}(n\theta)\boldsymbol{k}=\boldsymbol{q}^\top\mathbf{R}\big((n-m)\theta\big)\boldsymbol{k}.(R(mθ)q)⊤(R(nθ)k)=q⊤R(−mθ)R(nθ)k=q⊤R((n−m)θ)k. The absolute positions have cancelled; only n−mn-mn−m survives. For a dkd_kdk​-dimensional head (even dkd_kdk​), split coordinates into dk/2d_k/2dk​/2 pairs and rotate pair iii by its own frequency θi=10000−2i/dk\theta_i=10000^{-2i/d_k}θi​=10000−2i/dk​, i.e. use the block-diagonal rotation Rm=diag(R(mθ0),…,R(mθdk/2−1))\mathbf{R}_m=\text{diag}\big(\mathbf{R}(m\theta_0),\dots,\mathbf{R}(m\theta_{d_k/2-1})\big)Rm​=diag(R(mθ0​),…,R(mθdk​/2−1​)). Then ⟨Rmq,Rnk⟩=q⊤Rn−mk\langle\mathbf{R}_m\boldsymbol{q},\mathbf{R}_n\boldsymbol{k}\rangle=\boldsymbol{q}^\top\mathbf{R}_{n-m}\boldsymbol{k}⟨Rm​q,Rn​k⟩=q⊤Rn−m​k. ■\blacksquare■

In complex notation, treat pair iii as z=x2i+i x2i+1z=x_{2i}+\mathrm{i}\,x_{2i+1}z=x2i​+ix2i+1​; rotation is multiplication by eimθie^{\mathrm{i}m\theta_i}eimθi​, and the pair's contribution to the score is Re[qikˉi ei(m−n)θi]\mathrm{Re}\big[q_i\bar k_i\,e^{\mathrm{i}(m-n)\theta_i}\big]Re[qi​kˉi​ei(m−n)θi​].

Properties that make RoPE attractive:

  • No extra parameters and no change to the residual stream: it is applied to Q\mathbf{Q}Q and K\mathbf{K}K inside each attention layer, not added to the embeddings. Values are not rotated.
  • Relative by construction, yet computed as a cheap element-wise operation (pairs of multiplications by precomputed cosines and sines), compatible with fused attention kernels and with KV caching (cached keys already carry their own position).
  • Decay with distance of the score contributions of high-frequency pairs (the chart above), a useful inductive bias for locality.
  • Length extrapolation is imperfect. Beyond the training length the rotation angles take values never seen, and quality degrades. The common remedies rescale positions or frequencies: position interpolation (Chen et al., 2023) compresses positions m→m⋅Ltrain/Lnewm\to m\cdot L_\text{train}/L_\text{new}m→m⋅Ltrain​/Lnew​ and a short fine-tune restores quality; NTK-aware scaling and YaRN (Peng et al., 2023) rescale frequencies non-uniformly.
pythonrope.py
import torch

def rope_cache(T, dk, base=10000.0, device=None):
    """cos, sin tables of shape (T, dk/2)."""
    inv = 1.0 / (base ** (torch.arange(0, dk, 2, device=device).float() / dk))   # (dk/2,) theta_i
    ang = torch.outer(torch.arange(T, device=device).float(), inv)               # (T, dk/2) m * theta_i
    return ang.cos(), ang.sin()

def apply_rope(x, cos, sin):
    """x: (B, h, T, dk). Rotates each consecutive pair (x[2i], x[2i+1]) by m * theta_i."""
    x1, x2 = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]                  # (B, h, T, dk/2) each
    c, s = cos[: x.shape[-2]], sin[: x.shape[-2]]        # (T, dk/2), broadcast over B, h
    r1 = x1 * c - x2 * s
    r2 = x1 * s + x2 * c
    return torch.stack((r1, r2), dim=-1).flatten(-2)     # interleave back -> (B, h, T, dk)

# test: scores depend only on the relative offset
torch.manual_seed(0)
dk, T = 64, 32
cos, sin = rope_cache(T, dk)
q0, k0 = torch.randn(dk), torch.randn(dk)
Q = q0.expand(1, 1, T, dk).clone()                       # same raw q at every position
K = k0.expand(1, 1, T, dk).clone()
Qr, Kr = apply_rope(Q, cos, sin), apply_rope(K, cos, sin)
s = Qr[0, 0] @ Kr[0, 0].T                                # (T, T) score between positions
print(torch.allclose(s[5, 3], s[20, 18], atol=1e-4))     # same offset (2): True
print(torch.allclose(s[5, 3], s[5, 2], atol=1e-4))       # different offset: False

ALiBi

ALiBi (Press, Smith and Lewis, "Train Short, Test Long", 2021/2022) removes positional vectors entirely. It subtracts a penalty proportional to distance from each logit:

smn=qm⊤kndk−λr (m−n),n≤m,λr=2−8r/H (r=1,…,H).s_{mn} = \frac{\boldsymbol{q}_m^\top\boldsymbol{k}_n}{\sqrt{d_k}} - \lambda_r\,(m-n),\qquad n\le m,\qquad \lambda_r = 2^{-8r/H}\ (r=1,\dots,H).smn​=dk​​qm⊤​kn​​−λr​(m−n),n≤m,λr​=2−8r/H (r=1,…,H).

Head rrr has a fixed slope λr\lambda_rλr​ (none are learned): steep slopes make a head local, shallow slopes let it see far. The authors showed that models trained on 1024 tokens could extrapolate to roughly twice that length at inference with unchanged perplexity, outperforming sinusoidal and learned encodings in that test. Empirically RoPE with scaling has been more widely adopted, but ALiBi (used in BLOOM and MPT) is the simplest scheme to implement: add a precomputed bias matrix to the scores.

Choosing a scheme

Scheme Where applied Params Relative? Extrapolates? Used by
Sinusoidal embeddings (input) 0 approximately weak in practice original Transformer
Learned absolute embeddings (input) Tmax⁡dT_{\max} dTmax​d no no BERT, GPT-2
Relative bias attention scores small yes moderate T5, Transformer-XL
RoPE Q,K\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K}Q,K each layer 0 yes with scaling LLaMA-family, Qwen, Gemma
ALiBi attention scores 0 yes good BLOOM, MPT

A modern default is RoPE. Note what is not here: the causal mask itself leaks position information (token iii sees exactly iii predecessors), and some decoder-only models with no explicit position encoding at all ("NoPE") still learn order from it, a fact worth remembering when you debug.

Encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder models

The same block (attention, FFN, residuals, norms) can be assembled in three ways, distinguished by which attention masks they use and what they are trained to do.

Encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa). Bidirectional self-attention: every token sees the whole input. Output: a contextual vector for each token. Ideal for understanding tasks where the full input is available (classification, tagging, retrieval embeddings). It cannot generate text left to right because it has no autoregressive factorization. Trained with masked language modeling (Week 10).

Decoder-only (GPT family, LLaMA, most chat models). Causal self-attention: token iii sees tokens ≤i\le i≤i. Trained to predict the next token, which gives a proper joint distribution p(x1,…,xT)=∏tp(xt∣x<t)p(x_1,\dots,x_T)=\prod_t p(x_t\mid x_{<t})p(x1​,…,xT​)=∏t​p(xt​∣x<t​). Generates by sampling one token at a time, feeding it back in. It is the simplest design, uses every position as a training signal, and scales well, which is why it dominates large language models.

Encoder-decoder (original Transformer, T5, BART, many speech and translation systems). The encoder reads the input bidirectionally; the decoder generates the output causally while cross-attending to the encoder output. Natural for sequence-to-sequence problems with a clear input/output split (translation, summarization). It spends parameters on two stacks and cross-attention.

Between them lies the prefix-LM: a single stack where the first part (the prompt or prefix) is attended bidirectionally and the rest causally (rightmost panel of the figure above). It gives an encoder's richer representation of the prompt at the cost of one shared stack.

Causal masking in detail

For autoregressive training we want to compute the loss at all TTT positions in one parallel pass, so position iii must not see tokens j>ij>ij>i. The trick: before the softmax, set the forbidden score entries to −∞-\infty−∞, so they receive weight exactly zero:

s~ij={sijj≤i−∞j>i⇒αij=0 for j>i.\tilde s_{ij}=\begin{cases}s_{ij}&j\le i\\-\infty&j>i\end{cases}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \alpha_{ij}=0\ \text{for }j>i.s~ij​={sij​−∞​j≤ij>i​⇒αij​=0 for j>i.

Every row still has at least one finite entry (the diagonal), so no row is all −∞-\infty−∞ (which would produce NaNs). With a padding mask the situation is different: if a sequence is padded to the batch length, padded key positions must be masked for every query (a mask over the key axis, shape (B, 1, 1, T)), and padded query rows can be ignored in the loss. Combine masks with logical AND on booleans.

The causal mask is what makes teacher forcing efficient: given the whole target sequence, one forward pass produces the next-token predictions for every prefix at once. It is also why generation is different at inference time: new tokens arrive one at a time, and recomputing all earlier keys and values at each step would waste work, hence the KV cache (next section).

pythonmasks.py
import torch

T, B = 5, 2
causal = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool))              # (T, T); True = allowed
lengths = torch.tensor([5, 3])                                       # true lengths in the batch
keep = torch.arange(T)[None, :] < lengths[:, None]                   # (B, T); True = real token
pad_mask = keep[:, None, None, :]                                    # (B, 1, 1, T) over keys
mask = causal[None, None] & pad_mask                                 # (B, 1, T, T)
print(mask[1, 0].int())
# row i: ones up to min(i, 2) (columns 3, 4 are padding for the second sequence)
# every row still has a True on or left of the diagonal for real tokens
scores = torch.randn(B, 1, T, T)
weights = scores.masked_fill(~mask, float("-inf")).softmax(-1)       # padded query rows 3, 4:
print(torch.isnan(weights).any().item())                             # False here: causal keeps col 0

Computational cost and efficient attention

Counting the cost of a layer

Count multiply-adds as 2 FLOPs. For sequence length nnn and width ddd (one sequence, ignoring biases and normalization):

FLOPs of one Transformer layer
  • Q, K, V projections: three matrix products (n×d)(d×d)(n\times d)(d\times d)(n×d)(d×d): 3⋅2nd2=6nd23\cdot 2nd^2=6nd^23⋅2nd2=6nd2.
  • Scores QK⊤\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\topQK⊤ across all heads: hhh products (n×dk)(dk×n)(n\times d_k)(d_k\times n)(n×dk​)(dk​×n): 2n2dkh=2n2d2n^2 d_k h = 2n^2d2n2dk​h=2n2d.
  • Weighted values AV\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}AV: another 2n2d2n^2d2n2d.
  • Output projection: 2nd22nd^22nd2.
  • FFN with dff=4dd_\text{ff}=4ddff​=4d: two products, 2⋅2n⋅d⋅4d=16nd22\cdot 2n\cdot d\cdot4d=16nd^22⋅2n⋅d⋅4d=16nd2.

Total:   24 nd2⏟linear in n+4 n2d⏟quadratic in n.\;\underbrace{24\,n d^2}_{\text{linear in }n}+\underbrace{4\,n^2 d}_{\text{quadratic in }n}.linear in n24nd2​​+quadratic in n4n2d​​. The quadratic term equals the linear one when 4n2d=24nd24n^2d=24nd^24n2d=24nd2, i.e. at n=6dn=6dn=6d. For d=768d=768d=768 that is n=4608n=4608n=4608; for d=12288d=12288d=12288 (GPT-3 scale) it is n≈74,000n\approx 74{,}000n≈74,000.

So at the context lengths of the original paper (n≈50n\approx 50n≈50 to 500500500, d=512d=512d=512) attention is a minor part of the FLOPs, and the FFN and projections dominate. The quadratic term only becomes the bottleneck at long contexts:

But FLOPs understate the problem. Two further costs grow as n2n^2n2:

  • Memory for the score matrix. Materializing S∈Rh×n×n\mathbf{S}\in\R^{h\times n\times n}S∈Rh×n×n for n=8192n=8192n=8192, h=32h=32h=32 in 16-bit precision takes 32⋅81922⋅2≈4.332\cdot8192^2\cdot2\approx4.332⋅81922⋅2≈4.3 GB per layer per batch element (plus the same again for the softmax output, plus saved activations for backward).
  • Memory traffic. On a GPU, attention at moderate dkd_kdk​ is limited by reading and writing these n×nn\times nn×n tensors to slow high-bandwidth memory, not by arithmetic.

FlashAttention (Dao, Fu, Ermon, Rudra and Ré, 2022) attacks the second cost without approximation. It computes attention in tiles that fit in fast on-chip SRAM, maintaining a running maximum and running denominator for each row (the "online softmax" trick), so the n×nn\times nn×n matrix is never written to main memory. The result is the exact same output, with memory linear in nnn and a substantial wall-clock speedup. FLOPs are still O(n2d)O(n^2d)O(n2d). In PyTorch you obtain it through F.scaled_dot_product_attention. This is the pragmatic first answer to "attention is quadratic": use an exact IO-aware kernel before reaching for approximations.

The KV cache and the cost of generation

At inference a decoder generates token ttt given t−1t-1t−1 previous tokens. The keys and values of earlier tokens do not change (the mask forbids them from seeing the future), so we cache them. Each new step computes qt,kt,vt\boldsymbol{q}_t,\boldsymbol{k}_t,\boldsymbol{v}_tqt​,kt​,vt​ for the new token only, appends kt,vt\boldsymbol{k}_t,\boldsymbol{v}_tkt​,vt​ to the cache, and attends over all cached entries: O(td)O(td)O(td) work per step rather than O(t2d)O(t^2d)O(t2d). The cost is memory: 2⋅L⋅n⋅d2\cdot L\cdot n\cdot d2⋅L⋅n⋅d numbers. For L=32L=32L=32, d=4096d=4096d=4096, n=4096n=4096n=4096 in 16-bit precision that is 2⋅32⋅4096⋅4096⋅22\cdot32\cdot4096\cdot4096\cdot 22⋅32⋅4096⋅4096⋅2 bytes ≈2.1\approx 2.1≈2.1 GB per sequence, so the KV cache, not the weights, often limits serving throughput. Multi-query attention (Shazeer, 2019) shares one K/V head across all query heads, and grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) shares one K/V head per group of query heads, shrinking the cache by the group factor at small quality cost; both are standard in recent models.

Sparse and sliding-window attention

If each token attends to only O(1)O(1)O(1) or O(n)O(\sqrt n)O(n​) others, cost drops from n2n^2n2 to nnn or nnn\sqrt nnn​. The question is which entries to keep.

  • Sliding-window (local) attention: token iii attends to the www nearest tokens. Cost O(nw)O(nw)O(nw). Locality matches most of language, and stacking layers grows the effective receptive field: after LLL layers with a one-sided window www, information can travel L(w−1)L(w-1)L(w−1) positions. Longformer (Beltagy, Peters and Cohan, 2020) and Mistral 7B (Jiang et al., 2023) use sliding windows.
  • Dilated / strided patterns: attend to every sss-th token plus a local neighborhood, so a few layers cover long distances. Sparse Transformers (Child, Gray, Radford and Sutskever, 2019) factorize attention into a local head and a strided head with s≈ns\approx\sqrt ns≈n​, giving O(nn)O(n\sqrt n)O(nn​).
  • Global tokens: a few special tokens attend to and are attended by everyone (a [CLS] token, or task-specific question tokens in Longformer), providing a shortcut for global information. BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) combines window, global and random connections and proves the pattern retains the expressive power of full attention under certain assumptions.
  • Hashing / clustering (Reformer, Kitaev, Kaiser and Levskaya, 2020, using locality-sensitive hashing): attend only within buckets of similar queries and keys.

The practical price: custom sparse kernels, less hardware efficiency than dense attention (a sparse FLOP is slower than a dense FLOP), and, for fixed patterns, no way to attend to arbitrary far tokens in one layer. In practice many production LLMs keep full attention within a context length (extended by RoPE scaling) and use FlashAttention and GQA, while some interleave local and global layers.

Linear attention

The softmax is what forces us to form the n×nn\times nn×n matrix. If we replace exp⁡(q⊤k)\exp(\boldsymbol{q}^\top\boldsymbol{k})exp(q⊤k) with a kernel ϕ(q)⊤ϕ(k)\phi(\boldsymbol{q})^\top\phi(\boldsymbol{k})ϕ(q)⊤ϕ(k) for a feature map ϕ:Rdk→Rm\phi:\R^{d_k}\to\R^{m}ϕ:Rdk​→Rm, associativity lets us regroup the products.

Linear attention and its recurrent form

Define αij=ϕ(qi)⊤ϕ(kj) / ∑lϕ(qi)⊤ϕ(kl)\alpha_{ij}=\phi(\boldsymbol{q}_i)^\top\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_j)\,/\,\sum_l\phi(\boldsymbol{q}_i)^\top\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_l)αij​=ϕ(qi​)⊤ϕ(kj​)/∑l​ϕ(qi​)⊤ϕ(kl​). Then oi=∑jαijvj=ϕ(qi)⊤(∑jϕ(kj)vj⊤)ϕ(qi)⊤(∑lϕ(kl)).\boldsymbol{o}_i=\sum_j\alpha_{ij}\boldsymbol{v}_j=\frac{\phi(\boldsymbol{q}_i)^\top\Big(\sum_j\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_j)\boldsymbol{v}_j^\top\Big)}{\phi(\boldsymbol{q}_i)^\top\Big(\sum_l\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_l)\Big)}.oi​=j∑​αij​vj​=ϕ(qi​)⊤(∑l​ϕ(kl​))ϕ(qi​)⊤(∑j​ϕ(kj​)vj⊤​)​. The matrix S=∑jϕ(kj)vj⊤∈Rm×dv\mathbf{S}=\sum_j\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_j)\boldsymbol{v}_j^\top\in\R^{m\times d_v}S=∑j​ϕ(kj​)vj⊤​∈Rm×dv​ and the vector z=∑lϕ(kl)∈Rm\boldsymbol{z}=\sum_l\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_l)\in\R^mz=∑l​ϕ(kl​)∈Rm are computed once and shared by all queries, so the total cost is O(n m dv)O(n\,m\,d_v)O(nmdv​), linear in nnn. For a causal model restrict the sums to j≤ij\le ij≤i: Si=Si−1+ϕ(ki)vi⊤,zi=zi−1+ϕ(ki),oi=Si⊤ϕ(qi)zi⊤ϕ(qi).\mathbf{S}_i=\mathbf{S}_{i-1}+\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_i)\boldsymbol{v}_i^\top,\qquad \boldsymbol{z}_i=\boldsymbol{z}_{i-1}+\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_i),\qquad \boldsymbol{o}_i=\frac{\mathbf{S}_i^\top\phi(\boldsymbol{q}_i)}{\boldsymbol{z}_i^\top\phi(\boldsymbol{q}_i)}.Si​=Si−1​+ϕ(ki​)vi⊤​,zi​=zi−1​+ϕ(ki​),oi​=zi⊤​ϕ(qi​)Si⊤​ϕ(qi​)​. This is a recurrent network with a matrix-valued state of fixed size m×dvm\times d_vm×dv​, evaluated in parallel during training: the title "Transformers are RNNs" (Katharopoulos, Vyas, Pappas and Fleuret, 2020) refers to exactly this identity. Their feature map was ϕ(x)=elu(x)+1\phi(x)=\text{elu}(x)+1ϕ(x)=elu(x)+1 (positive, so the weights are valid); Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021) uses random features to approximate the softmax kernel.

Linear attention achieves constant memory per generated token, but it compresses the entire past into a fixed-size state, so it is a lossy memory, and in practice it has trailed softmax attention in quality on tasks that need precise recall. Its descendants (state-space models such as Mamba, Gu and Dao 2023, and gated linear recurrences) revisit this trade-off; see the discussion in Week 16. Linformer (Wang et al., 2020) takes a different route: project the nnn keys and values to a fixed k≪nk\ll nk≪n using learned low-rank maps. The summary: exact + efficient kernels (FlashAttention, KV cache, GQA) are the baseline; approximate patterns are chosen when context is very long or memory is tight.

Counting parameters and FLOPs

Parameters per layer

Take a standard pre-norm decoder block with width ddd, FFN width 4d4d4d, learned biases, and two LayerNorms:

  • attention: WQ,WK,WV,WO\mathbf{W}_Q,\mathbf{W}_K,\mathbf{W}_V,\mathbf{W}_OWQ​,WK​,WV​,WO​: 4d24d^24d2 weights plus 4d4d4d biases;
  • FFN: d⋅4d+4d⋅d=8d2d\cdot4d+4d\cdot d=8d^2d⋅4d+4d⋅d=8d2 weights plus 4d+d=5d4d+d=5d4d+d=5d biases;
  • two LayerNorms: 2⋅2d=4d2\cdot2d=4d2⋅2d=4d.

So a block has 12d2+13d12d^2+13d12d2+13d parameters, and LLL blocks give 12Ld2+13Ld12Ld^2+13Ld12Ld2+13Ld. Add the token embedding VdVdVd (shared with the output head when weights are tied), a learned position table Tmax⁡dT_{\max} dTmax​d if used, and the final LayerNorm 2d2d2d:

N  =  12Ld2+13Ld+(V+Tmax⁡)d+2d.N \;=\; 12Ld^2+13Ld+(V+T_{\max})d+2d.N=12Ld2+13Ld+(V+Tmax​)d+2d.

For GPT-2 small (L=12L=12L=12, d=768d=768d=768, V=50257V=50257V=50257, Tmax⁡=1024T_{\max}=1024Tmax​=1024): 12⋅12⋅7682=84.912\cdot12\cdot768^2=84.912⋅12⋅7682=84.9M, plus 13⋅12⋅768≈0.1213\cdot12\cdot768\approx0.1213⋅12⋅768≈0.12M, plus 51281⋅768=39.451281\cdot768=39.451281⋅768=39.4M, giving 124.4M, the published 124M. The "12Ld212Ld^212Ld2" term is the one to remember: non-embedding parameters ≈12Ld2\approx 12Ld^2≈12Ld2.

Use the calculator to check your own arithmetic against the presets, and to see how vocabulary size and learned positions matter for small models.
