Training FLOPs: the 6N rule

A matrix multiply of an m×km\times km×k matrix by a k×nk\times nk×n matrix costs 2mkn2mkn2mkn FLOPs. A token passing through all weight matrices of the model does one multiply-add per weight, so the forward pass costs about 2N2N2N FLOPs per token (NNN counting matrix-multiplied weights; embedding lookups are free but the output head VdVdVd is a real matmul). The backward pass computes two products per weight matrix (the gradient with respect to the input, and with respect to the weights), each the size of the forward product, so it costs about 4N4N4N. Forward plus backward gives the widely used estimate

C  ≈  6 N DFLOPs to train on D tokens,C \;\approx\; 6\,N\,D\quad\text{FLOPs to train on }D\text{ tokens},C≈6NDFLOPs to train on D tokens,

which ignores the attention-score term ≈12 L n d\approx 12\,L\,n\,d≈12Lnd per token (forward and backward) that matters only when n≳dn\gtrsim dn≳d. GPT-2 small on 10 billion tokens costs about 6⋅1.24×108⋅1010≈7.5×10186\cdot1.24\times10^8\cdot10^{10}\approx7.5\times10^{18}6⋅1.24×108⋅1010≈7.5×1018 FLOPs: at a realistic 40% utilization of a 300 TFLOP/s accelerator (120 TFLOP/s effective) that is about 17 hours on one device. This rule is the basis of the scaling-law analysis in Week 10.

Memory budget of training

For mixed-precision training with Adam, each parameter costs roughly 16 bytes: 2 for the bf16/fp16 weight, 2 for its gradient, and 12 for fp32 master weight, first moment and second moment (4 + 4 + 4). A 7-billion-parameter model therefore needs about 112 GB of state before activations, which is why large models shard optimizer state (ZeRO/FSDP, Week 16).

Training Transformers

Transformers are notoriously sensitive to optimization details. The recipe below is a compact summary of what practitioners converge on; each item has a reason, not only a tradition.

Optimizer: AdamW and its betas

Use Adam with decoupled weight decay (AdamW, Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019). The original paper used β2=0.98\beta_2=0.98β2​=0.98, ϵ=10−9\epsilon=10^{-9}ϵ=10−9; most LLM recipes use β2=0.95\beta_2=0.95β2​=0.95 (a shorter memory of squared gradients reacts faster to the loss spikes that large models exhibit), ϵ≈10−8\epsilon\approx10^{-8}ϵ≈10−8, weight decay 0.10.10.1 applied to weight matrices but not to biases, LayerNorm gains or embeddings, and gradient-norm clipping at 1.0.

Learning-rate warmup

Almost every Transformer recipe increases the learning rate linearly from near zero over the first few hundred to few thousand steps. Why?

  1. Adam's second-moment estimate is unreliable at the start. After a few steps v^t\hat v_tv^t​ is computed from very few gradients, so the effective per-parameter step η m^t/v^t\eta\,\hat m_t/\sqrt{\hat v_t}ηm^t​/v^t​​ can be wildly too large for some parameters. Liu et al. (2020, "On the Variance of the Adaptive Learning Rate and Beyond", RAdam) give this analysis and show that warmup is a heuristic cure for the high variance of the adaptive learning rate early on.
  2. Post-norm layers have large initial gradients near the output (Xiong et al., 2020). A big step in a badly conditioned region can push the model into a bad basin it never leaves. Pre-norm substantially reduces this need for warmup, though large models still use it.
  3. Attention is sharp at initialization for some heads, and large early updates can saturate softmaxes.

The original paper's schedule, η(t)=dmodel−0.5min⁡(t−0.5, t⋅twarm−1.5)\eta(t)=d_\text{model}^{-0.5}\min(t^{-0.5},\,t\cdot t_\text{warm}^{-1.5})η(t)=dmodel−0.5​min(t−0.5,t⋅twarm−1.5​) with twarm=4000t_\text{warm}=4000twarm​=4000, rises linearly and then decays as 1/t1/\sqrt t1/t​. Modern LLM recipes prefer linear warmup followed by cosine decay to about 10% of the peak (Week 3).

Label smoothing

For a vocabulary of VVV classes the one-hot target pushes the model's logit for the correct class toward infinity. Label smoothing (Szegedy et al., 2016; used in the Transformer paper with ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1ϵ=0.1) replaces the target by qc=(1−ϵ) 1[c=y]+ϵ/Vq_c=(1-\epsilon)\,\mathbb 1[c=y]+\epsilon/Vqc​=(1−ϵ)1[c=y]+ϵ/V. The loss becomes a mix of the usual cross-entropy and a cross-entropy against the uniform distribution:

L=(1−ϵ) (−log⁡py)+ϵ⋅(−1V∑clog⁡pc).\mathcal{L}=(1-\epsilon)\,\big(-\log p_y\big)+\epsilon\cdot\Big(-\frac1V\sum_c\log p_c\Big).L=(1−ϵ)(−logpy​)+ϵ⋅(−V1​c∑​logpc​).

The effect on a translation model was a worse perplexity (the model is deliberately less confident) but a better BLEU score, because better calibrated outputs make beam search work better. For modern pretraining of decoder-only LLMs it is usually omitted. In PyTorch: F.cross_entropy(logits, y, label_smoothing=0.1).

Mixed precision

Matrix multiplications on modern GPUs run several times faster in 16-bit formats, and 16-bit tensors halve memory. There are two formats, and the difference matters:

Format Exponent bits Mantissa bits Range Notes
fp32 8 23 about 10±3810^{\pm38}10±38 reference
fp16 5 10 max 65504, min normal about 6×10−56\times10^{-5}6×10−5 more precise but narrow range; needs loss scaling
bf16 8 7 same range as fp32 coarser precision, no loss scaling needed

With fp16, gradients smaller than about 6×10−86\times10^{-8}6×10−8 underflow to zero; dynamic loss scaling (Micikevicius et al., 2018) multiplies the loss by a large factor before backward and divides the gradients afterwards, lowering the scale when an overflow (inf/NaN) is detected. bf16 has the exponent range of fp32 and therefore needs none of this, which is why it is the default on hardware that supports it (A100/H100, TPUs, recent consumer GPUs). The rule of thumb: keep weights' master copy, optimizer state, softmax, normalization statistics and the loss in fp32; run matmuls in 16-bit. PyTorch's torch.autocast automates the choices.

pythonamp.py
import torch

def train_step(model, opt, scaler, x, y, use_bf16=True):
    # autocast chooses 16-bit for matmuls and keeps reductions/softmax/loss in fp32
    dtype = torch.bfloat16 if use_bf16 else torch.float16
    with torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=dtype):
        _, loss = model(x, y)
    if use_bf16:
        loss.backward()                                  # no scaler needed for bf16
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        opt.step()
    else:
        scaler.scale(loss).backward()                    # fp16: scale to avoid underflow
        scaler.unscale_(opt)                             # unscale BEFORE clipping
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        scaler.step(opt)                                 # skips the step if grads have inf/NaN
        scaler.update()
    opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    return loss.item()

# scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler("cuda")   # only needed for fp16

Dropout, initialization and other details

  • Dropout of 0.1 on attention weights, sublayer outputs and embeddings was standard for small supervised models; large pretrained models trained for a single epoch on huge corpora often use none, because overfitting is not the issue (Week 4).
  • Initialization: normal with standard deviation 0.02 for weights (GPT-2), and for the output projections that write into the residual stream, a scale of 0.02/2L0.02/\sqrt{2L}0.02/2L​ so that the stream's variance does not grow with depth (each of the 2L2L2L sublayers adds a term).
  • Batch size in tokens: hundreds of thousands to millions for large runs; use gradient accumulation if memory-limited.
  • Loss spikes: occasionally the loss jumps and may or may not recover. Remedies are lowering the learning rate, skipping the offending batch, restarting from an earlier checkpoint, QK-norm, and keeping softmax and logits in fp32.

Lab: a GPT from scratch in PyTorch

We now assemble every piece into a small GPT-style decoder (about 800k parameters), train it as a character-level language model on a tiny corpus, and sample text. The structure mirrors Karpathy's nanoGPT, which you should read afterwards. A GPU makes it fast (about two minutes on a Colab T4), but it also runs on CPU with smaller settings.

Step 1: data

pythonlab_data.py
import os, urllib.request, torch

URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/char-rnn/master/data/tinyshakespeare/input.txt"
if not os.path.exists("input.txt"):
    try:
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(URL, "input.txt")
    except Exception:                                   # offline fallback: tiny repeated corpus
        text = ("to be or not to be that is the question\n"
                "whether tis nobler in the mind to suffer\n") * 200
        open("input.txt", "w").write(text)
text = open("input.txt", encoding="utf-8").read()
chars = sorted(set(text))                                # character vocabulary
V = len(chars)
stoi = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(chars)}
itos = {i: c for c, i in stoi.items()}
encode = lambda s: [stoi[c] for c in s]
decode = lambda ids: "".join(itos[i] for i in ids)

data = torch.tensor(encode(text), dtype=torch.long)
n_train = int(0.9 * len(data))
train_data, val_data = data[:n_train], data[n_train:]
print(f"{len(text):,} chars, vocab {V}")                 # ~1.1M chars, vocab 65 for tinyshakespeare

def get_batch(split, B, T, device):
    d = train_data if split == "train" else val_data
    ix = torch.randint(len(d) - T - 1, (B,))             # random start offsets
    x = torch.stack([d[i : i + T] for i in ix])          # (B, T) inputs
    y = torch.stack([d[i + 1 : i + T + 1] for i in ix])  # (B, T) targets = inputs shifted by one
    return x.to(device), y.to(device)

xb, yb = get_batch("train", 4, 8, "cpu")
print(xb.shape, yb.shape)                                # torch.Size([4, 8]) torch.Size([4, 8])

Step 2: the model

pythonlab_model.py
import math
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, h, dropout):
        super().__init__()
        assert d % h == 0
        self.h, self.dk = h, d // h
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d, 3 * d, bias=False)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(d, d, bias=False)
        self.dropout = dropout
        self.resid_drop = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, x):                                  # x: (B, T, d)
        B, T, d = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).split(d, dim=2)
        q, k, v = (t.view(B, T, self.h, self.dk).transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v))  # (B,h,T,dk)
        y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True,
                                           dropout_p=self.dropout if self.training else 0.0)
        y = y.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, T, d)   # (B, T, d)
        return self.resid_drop(self.proj(y))

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, dropout):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1, self.fc2 = nn.Linear(d, 4 * d, bias=False), nn.Linear(4 * d, d, bias=False)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.drop(self.fc2(F.gelu(self.fc1(x))))

class Block(nn.Module):                                    # pre-norm Transformer block
    def __init__(self, d, h, dropout):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln1, self.attn = nn.LayerNorm(d), CausalSelfAttention(d, h, dropout)
        self.ln2, self.mlp = nn.LayerNorm(d), MLP(d, dropout)
    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x))                     # communicate
        x = x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x))                      # compute
        return x

class GPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab, block_size=128, n_layer=4, n_head=4, d=128, dropout=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.block_size = block_size
        self.tok = nn.Embedding(vocab, d)
        self.pos = nn.Embedding(block_size, d)             # learned absolute positions
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(Block(d, n_head, dropout) for _ in range(n_layer))
        self.ln_f = nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.head = nn.Linear(d, vocab, bias=False)
        self.head.weight = self.tok.weight                 # weight tying
        self.apply(self._init)
        for name, p in self.named_parameters():            # scaled init for residual writers
            if name.endswith("proj.weight") or name.endswith("fc2.weight"):
                nn.init.normal_(p, mean=0.0, std=0.02 / math.sqrt(2 * n_layer))

    @staticmethod
    def _init(m):
        if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
            nn.init.normal_(m.weight, 0.0, 0.02)
        elif isinstance(m, nn.Embedding):
            nn.init.normal_(m.weight, 0.0, 0.02)

    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):                  # idx: (B, T) int64
        B, T = idx.shape
        assert T <= self.block_size
        pos = torch.arange(T, device=idx.device)           # (T,)
        x = self.drop(self.tok(idx) + self.pos(pos))       # (B, T, d)
        for blk in self.blocks:
            x = blk(x)
        logits = self.head(self.ln_f(x))                   # (B, T, V)
        loss = None
        if targets is not None:
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)), targets.view(-1))
        return logits, loss

    @torch.no_grad()
    def generate(self, idx, max_new_tokens, temperature=1.0, top_k=None):
        self.eval()
        for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
            ctx = idx[:, -self.block_size:]                # crop to the context window
            logits, _ = self(ctx)
            logits = logits[:, -1, :] / max(temperature, 1e-6)       # (B, V) last position only
            if top_k is not None:
                kth = torch.topk(logits, min(top_k, logits.size(-1))).values[:, [-1]]
                logits = logits.masked_fill(logits < kth, float("-inf"))
            probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
            nxt = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1)  # (B, 1)
            idx = torch.cat([idx, nxt], dim=1)
        return idx

model = GPT(vocab=65)
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"{n_params/1e6:.2f}M parameters")                   # ~0.82M (tied head counted once)

Two sanity checks before training. First, the initial loss should be close to ln⁡V\ln VlnV (about 4.17 for V=65V=65V=65), because a model with tiny initial weights predicts a nearly uniform distribution. Second, a causality test: change a future token and verify that earlier logits are unchanged.

pythonlab_checks.py
import math, torch
model = GPT(vocab=65).eval()
x = torch.randint(0, 65, (2, 16))
_, loss = model(x, x)
print(loss.item(), math.log(65))                         # both close to 4.17

x2 = x.clone()
x2[:, 10] = (x2[:, 10] + 1) % 65                         # corrupt token at position 10
l1, _ = model(x)
l2, _ = model(x2)
print(torch.allclose(l1[:, :10], l2[:, :10], atol=1e-5))  # True: positions < 10 unaffected
print(torch.allclose(l1[:, 10:], l2[:, 10:], atol=1e-5))  # False: positions >= 10 changed

Step 3: training

pythonlab_train.py
import math, time, torch

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
torch.manual_seed(1337)
B, T = 64, 128
model = GPT(vocab=V, block_size=T, n_layer=4, n_head=4, d=128, dropout=0.1).to(device)

# weight decay only on matrices (ndim >= 2), not on biases/LayerNorm gains
decay = [p for p in model.parameters() if p.ndim >= 2]
no_decay = [p for p in model.parameters() if p.ndim < 2]
opt = torch.optim.AdamW([{"params": decay, "weight_decay": 0.1},
                         {"params": no_decay, "weight_decay": 0.0}],
                        lr=3e-3, betas=(0.9, 0.95))

max_steps, warmup, lr_max, lr_min = 2000, 100, 3e-3, 3e-4
def lr_at(step):
    if step < warmup:
        return lr_max * (step + 1) / warmup              # linear warmup
    t = (step - warmup) / (max_steps - warmup)
    return lr_min + 0.5 * (lr_max - lr_min) * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * t))   # cosine decay

@torch.no_grad()
def evaluate(n_batches=20):
    model.eval()
    out = {}
    for split in ("train", "val"):
        losses = torch.zeros(n_batches)
        for i in range(n_batches):
            x, y = get_batch(split, B, T, device)
            _, loss = model(x, y)
            losses[i] = loss.item()
        out[split] = losses.mean().item()
    model.train()
    return out

use_amp = device == "cuda"
t0 = time.time()
for step in range(max_steps + 1):
    for g in opt.param_groups:
        g["lr"] = lr_at(step)
    if step % 250 == 0:
        e = evaluate()
        print(f"step {step:4d} | train {e['train']:.3f} | val {e['val']:.3f} | {time.time()-t0:.0f}s")
    x, y = get_batch("train", B, T, device)
    with torch.autocast(device_type=device, dtype=torch.bfloat16, enabled=use_amp):
        _, loss = model(x, y)
    loss.backward()
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
    opt.step()
    opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)

On tinyshakespeare you should see the loss fall from about 4.2 at step 0 to roughly 1.6 to 1.8 on validation after 2000 steps (numbers vary with seed and hardware; a larger model with more steps reaches about 1.5). If your loss stays above 3, see the debugging checklist below.

text
step    0 | train 4.213 | val 4.209 | 1s
step  250 | train 2.431 | val 2.452 | 14s
step  500 | train 2.127 | val 2.175 | 27s
...
step 2000 | train 1.620 | val 1.742 | 105s

(Illustrative output; your numbers will differ in the second decimal.)

Step 4: generation and the effect of temperature

pythonlab_generate.py
prompt = torch.zeros((1, 1), dtype=torch.long, device=device)       # start from token id 0 (newline)
for temp, k in [(0.5, None), (1.0, None), (1.0, 10)]:
    out = model.generate(prompt, max_new_tokens=300, temperature=temp, top_k=k)
    print(f"--- temperature {temp}, top_k {k} ---")
    print(decode(out[0].tolist()))

Low temperature yields repetitive but locally well-formed text, temperature 1 samples from the model's actual distribution and produces more variety (and more typos), and top-kkk trims the improbable tail. Week 10 analyzes these decoding strategies carefully and gives an interactive playground.

Step 5: speed up generation with a KV cache (extension)

The generate method above recomputes everything for the whole context at each step. As an extension, modify CausalSelfAttention.forward to accept and return a (k, v) cache: when generating, feed only the newest token, concatenate its key and value to the cached ones along the time axis, and compute attention with is_causal=False (a single query attending to all cached keys is already causal). Remember to pass the correct absolute position to the position embedding. Check your implementation by asserting that the logits agree with the uncached path to within 10−510^{-5}10−5.

Common mistakes and debugging tips

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Loss is NaN from the first steps A row of the mask is all −∞-\infty−∞ (softmax of all −∞-\infty−∞); or fp16 overflow Ensure every query can attend to at least one key; use bf16 or a loss scaler; compute softmax in fp32
Loss decreases suspiciously fast to near zero Information leak: missing or wrong causal mask, or targets not shifted Run the causality test above; check y = x shifted by one
Loss stuck near ln⁡V\ln VlnV Learning rate too high or too low, no warmup, wrong init, forgot to call opt.step() or zero grads Overfit a single batch first; add warmup; lower LR
Loss good but generations are garbage model.eval() not set during generation (dropout active); wrong context cropping; temperature bug Call eval(); check that the last position's logits are sampled, not the first
Boolean/float mask confusion True means allowed in scaled_dot_product_attention but masked in nn.MultiheadAttention's attn_mask and key_padding_mask Read the docs for each API; write a unit test with a tiny known case
Padding tokens influence outputs Pad keys not masked Build a key padding mask; test that appending pads does not change non-pad outputs
Shapes are right but results wrong after reshaping heads Used view(B, h, T, dk) directly instead of view(B, T, h, dk).transpose(1, 2) The head split must keep each token's features contiguous; transpose after view
Out-of-memory at longer sequence O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) score matrices materialized Use fused SDPA, gradient checkpointing, smaller batch, shorter context
Model cannot use word order Position information missing, or added to the wrong tensor Verify that permuting input tokens changes the output
Training unstable at larger scale Post-norm without warmup, β2=0.999\beta_2=0.999β2​=0.999, attention logit growth Pre-norm, β2=0.95\beta_2=0.95β2​=0.95, grad clipping, QK-norm, lower LR
The three debugging tests every Transformer should pass
  1. Overfit one batch: loss should go to about zero within a few hundred steps.
  2. Initial loss ≈ln⁡V\approx\ln V≈lnV.
  3. Causality / invariance tests: changing future tokens must not change past logits; appending pad tokens must not change non-pad outputs.

Exercises

Exercise 1: variance and the scale factor (derivation)

Suppose queries and keys have i.i.d. components with mean 0 and variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, independent of each other. (a) What is Var⁡(q⊤k)\Var(\boldsymbol{q}^\top\boldsymbol{k})Var(q⊤k)? (b) What scaling factor restores unit variance? (c) After training, LayerNorm'd inputs and learned projections often give σ2≠1\sigma^2\ne1σ2=1. Why does the 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_k}1/dk​​ factor still matter?

Solution

(a) Each product qmkmq_mk_mqm​km​ has variance E[qm2]E[km2]=σ4\E[q_m^2]\E[k_m^2]=\sigma^4E[qm2​]E[km2​]=σ4, and the dkd_kdk​ terms are independent, so Var⁡=dkσ4\Var=d_k\sigma^4Var=dk​σ4. (b) Divide by σ2dk\sigma^2\sqrt{d_k}σ2dk​​; with σ=1\sigma=1σ=1 this is 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_k}1/dk​​. (c) The factor fixes the initial statistics so that training starts in a well-conditioned regime; the network can then learn larger or smaller effective temperatures through the norms of WQ,WK\mathbf{W}_Q,\mathbf{W}_KWQ​,WK​. Without it, the scale at initialization grows with dkd_kdk​ and the softmax saturates (gradients vanish) before the network has had a chance to adapt.

Input (4, 100, 768); after the fused QKV projection (4, 100, 2304), split into three (4, 100, 768); heads (4, 12, 100, 64); scores and probabilities (4, 12, 100, 100); weighted values (4, 12, 100, 64); merged (4, 100, 768); output (4, 100, 768). Parameters: 4⋅7682+4⋅768=2,362,3684\cdot768^2+4\cdot768=2{,}362{,}3684⋅7682+4⋅768=2,362,368. Attention probabilities: 4⋅12⋅100⋅100=480,0004\cdot12\cdot100\cdot100=480{,}0004⋅12⋅100⋅100=480,000 floats per layer (about 0.96 MB in fp16), which for n=8192n=8192n=8192 would be 4⋅12⋅81922≈3.2×1094\cdot 12\cdot 8192^2\approx3.2\times10^94⋅12⋅81922≈3.2×109 floats: the quadratic cost in action.

Exercise 3: implement masks (coding)

Write a function make_mask(lengths, T) returning a boolean (B, 1, T, T) tensor that combines a causal mask with a key padding mask for sequences of the given true lengths. Test that (i) future entries are False, (ii) padded keys are False for every query, and (iii) the output of MultiHeadAttention at non-pad positions is unchanged when you append extra pad tokens.

Solution
python
import torch
def make_mask(lengths, T):
    causal = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool))
    keep = torch.arange(T)[None, :] < lengths[:, None]       # (B, T)
    return causal[None, None] & keep[:, None, None, :]       # (B, 1, T, T)

lengths = torch.tensor([4, 2]); T = 6
m = make_mask(lengths, T)
assert not m[:, :, 0, 1].any()                               # future blocked
assert not m[1, 0, :, 2:].any()                              # padded keys blocked
# (iii) run MHA on a batch of length 4 and on the same batch padded to 6 with arbitrary
# values in the pad slots; the first 4 output rows must agree (atol 1e-5).

Note that query rows at pad positions may be all False when the sequence has zero real tokens before them; with a causal mask plus padding they still have key 0 allowed whenever the sequence has at least one real token, so no NaNs arise for non-empty sequences.

Exercise 4: RoPE and relative position (derivation)

Show that for the block-diagonal rotation Rm\mathbf{R}_mRm​ of RoPE, the attention score between a query at position mmm and a key at position nnn equals q⊤Rn−mk\boldsymbol{q}^\top\mathbf{R}_{n-m}\boldsymbol{k}q⊤Rn−m​k. Then show that the effect of this score on pair iii vanishes slowly for small θi\theta_iθi​ (low frequency) and oscillates fast for large θi\theta_iθi​, and explain why this gives a mixture of local and long-range sensitivity.

Solution

Rm\mathbf{R}_mRm​ is orthogonal with Rm⊤=R−m\mathbf{R}_m^\top=\mathbf{R}_{-m}Rm⊤​=R−m​ and RaRb=Ra+b\mathbf{R}_a\mathbf{R}_b=\mathbf{R}_{a+b}Ra​Rb​=Ra+b​ (block-wise rotations add angles). Therefore (Rmq)⊤(Rnk)=q⊤R−mRnk=q⊤Rn−mk(\mathbf{R}_m\boldsymbol{q})^\top(\mathbf{R}_n\boldsymbol{k})=\boldsymbol{q}^\top\mathbf{R}_{-m}\mathbf{R}_n\boldsymbol{k}=\boldsymbol{q}^\top\mathbf{R}_{n-m}\boldsymbol{k}(Rm​q)⊤(Rn​k)=q⊤R−m​Rn​k=q⊤Rn−m​k. Pair iii contributes ∥qi∥∥ki∥cos⁡(∠i+(n−m)θi)\|\boldsymbol{q}_i\|\|\boldsymbol{k}_i\|\cos(\angle_i+(n-m)\theta_i)∥qi​∥∥ki​∥cos(∠i​+(n−m)θi​), where ∠i\angle_i∠i​ is the angle between the unrotated pair vectors. For θi=1\theta_i=1θi​=1 the cosine cycles every 2π≈62\pi\approx62π≈6 positions: it can encode the exact small offset but aliases at larger ones. For θi=10000−1≈10−4\theta_i=10000^{-1}\approx10^{-4}θi​=10000−1≈10−4 the cosine changes appreciably only over thousands of positions: it carries coarse, long-range distance information. Together they are like the clocks in the sinusoidal encoding, now acting on the score.

Exercise 6: pre-norm versus post-norm experiment (coding)

Using the lab code, add a flag to switch Block to post-norm (x←LN(x+Sublayer(x))x\leftarrow\text{LN}(x+\text{Sublayer}(x))x←LN(x+Sublayer(x))). Train both variants with the same seed, six layers, a deliberately large learning rate of 3×10−33\times10^{-3}3×10−3 and no warmup, and then again with 200 warmup steps. Report the loss curves and explain what you see.

Solution

Expected outcome (to be verified by running): with no warmup and a high learning rate the post-norm model typically trains poorly or diverges, while the pre-norm model trains; with warmup both train, with post-norm often ending slightly worse or similar at this tiny scale. The explanation is the gradient-scale difference of the two placements described in the text. A minimal post-norm block is:

python
def forward(self, x):
    x = self.ln1(x + self.attn(x))
    return self.ln2(x + self.mlp(x))

(and drop the final ln_f, since each block already ends in a norm). Plot both curves with and without warmup and relate any divergence to the first 100 steps.

Exercise 7: what would happen if... (conceptual)

For each modification, predict the effect on a trained decoder-only LM and on training: (a) remove the positional encoding; (b) remove the causal mask but still train on next-token prediction; (c) apply RoPE to the values as well as queries and keys; (d) share all of WQ,WK,WV\mathbf{W}_Q,\mathbf{W}_K,\mathbf{W}_VWQ​,WK​,WV​ within a head.

Solution

(a) Content-only attention is permutation-equivariant, but the causal mask alone provides some order information (token iii sees exactly iii predecessors), so the model can still learn to some degree; it will be weaker at tasks that depend on exact offsets. In an encoder without a mask, the model becomes a bag-of-words model. (b) Each position can read its own target token (the next token is in its context), so the loss collapses toward zero in training and the model learns to copy, not to predict: generation then fails. This is the "leak" described in the pitfalls table. (c) Rotating values would make the output depend on absolute positions (the weighted sum would mix vectors rotated by different angles) and break relative-only behavior; RoPE is deliberately applied to Q\mathbf{Q}Q and K\mathbf{K}K only. (d) With WQ=WK\mathbf{W}_Q=\mathbf{W}_KWQ​=WK​ the score matrix XWW⊤X⊤\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^\top\mathbf{X}^\topXWW⊤X⊤ is symmetric, so token iii's affinity for jjj equals jjj's for iii (before the softmax), and a token always has high affinity with itself. That removes useful asymmetric relations (such as a verb looking for its subject but not vice versa) and reduces capacity.

Exercise 8: linear attention equals a recurrence (derivation, challenging)

Starting from oi=∑j≤iαijvj\boldsymbol{o}_i=\sum_{j\le i}\alpha_{ij}\boldsymbol{v}_joi​=∑j≤i​αij​vj​ with αij=ϕ(qi)⊤ϕ(kj)/∑l≤iϕ(qi)⊤ϕ(kl)\alpha_{ij}=\phi(\boldsymbol{q}_i)^\top\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_j)/\sum_{l\le i}\phi(\boldsymbol{q}_i)^\top\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_l)αij​=ϕ(qi​)⊤ϕ(kj​)/∑l≤i​ϕ(qi​)⊤ϕ(kl​), derive the recurrent form and compute the time and memory cost of generating TTT tokens, versus softmax attention with a KV cache. Then explain what information the fixed-size state cannot represent that a KV cache can.

Solution

Factor the numerator: ∑j≤iϕ(qi)⊤ϕ(kj)vj=(∑j≤ivjϕ(kj)⊤)ϕ(qi)=Si⊤ϕ(qi)\sum_{j\le i}\phi(\boldsymbol{q}_i)^\top\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_j)\boldsymbol{v}_j=\big(\sum_{j\le i}\boldsymbol{v}_j\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_j)^\top\big)\phi(\boldsymbol{q}_i)=\mathbf{S}_i^\top\phi(\boldsymbol{q}_i)∑j≤i​ϕ(qi​)⊤ϕ(kj​)vj​=(∑j≤i​vj​ϕ(kj​)⊤)ϕ(qi​)=Si⊤​ϕ(qi​) with Si=∑j≤iϕ(kj)vj⊤∈Rm×dv\mathbf{S}_i=\sum_{j\le i}\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_j)\boldsymbol{v}_j^\top\in\R^{m\times d_v}Si​=∑j≤i​ϕ(kj​)vj⊤​∈Rm×dv​, and the denominator is zi⊤ϕ(qi)\boldsymbol{z}_i^\top\phi(\boldsymbol{q}_i)zi⊤​ϕ(qi​) with zi=∑l≤iϕ(kl)\boldsymbol{z}_i=\sum_{l\le i}\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_l)zi​=∑l≤i​ϕ(kl​). Both satisfy Si=Si−1+ϕ(ki)vi⊤\mathbf{S}_i=\mathbf{S}_{i-1}+\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_i)\boldsymbol{v}_i^\topSi​=Si−1​+ϕ(ki​)vi⊤​ and zi=zi−1+ϕ(ki)\boldsymbol{z}_i=\boldsymbol{z}_{i-1}+\phi(\boldsymbol{k}_i)zi​=zi−1​+ϕ(ki​). Each step costs O(mdv)O(m d_v)O(mdv​) time, and memory is O(mdv)O(md_v)O(mdv​) independent of iii; generating TTT tokens costs O(Tmdv)O(Tmd_v)O(Tmdv​) time and O(mdv)O(md_v)O(mdv​) memory. With a KV cache, step ttt costs O(td)O(td)O(td) and the cache holds O(td)O(td)O(td) numbers, so total time O(T2d)O(T^2d)O(T2d) and memory growing linearly. The state S\mathbf{S}S is a sum of TTT rank-one terms compressed into m×dvm\times d_vm×dv​ numbers: when T≫mT\gg mT≫m the individual (kj,vj)(\boldsymbol{k}_j,\boldsymbol{v}_j)(kj​,vj​) pairs overlap in the state and exact recall of a specific old token (e.g. a rare name given 3000 tokens earlier) is not possible, whereas the KV cache keeps them all separate.

Exercise 9: break the position encoding (challenging, coding)

Train the lab GPT on a synthetic task where the target is the input sequence reversed (feed a random string of 16 digits, then a separator, and train the model to output the string reversed). Compare (i) learned absolute positions, (ii) no positions, and (iii) RoPE (apply apply_rope to Q\mathbf{Q}Q, K\mathbf{K}K in CausalSelfAttention and delete the position embedding). Which succeed, and why? Then test (i) and (iii) on strings of length 32.

Solution

Expected behavior (verify by running): the reversal task requires the model to attend to position 2T−i2T-i2T−i when writing token iii, a positional operation. With learned absolute positions or RoPE the model solves it for the training length; with no positions it can use only the causal-mask-induced counts and generally fails or does so slowly. At length 32, learned positions are undefined beyond the table (the table has only 16+1+16 entries unless you enlarge it, and untrained rows are random), so learned absolute positions cannot extrapolate. RoPE can generalize partially, but because the model learned frequencies for distances up to about 33 it can still degrade; this is the same length-extrapolation limitation discussed in the RoPE section.

Key takeaways

Key takeaways
  • Attention is a soft, differentiable dictionary lookup: output =softmax⁡(QK⊤/dk)V=\softmax(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top/\sqrt{d_k})\mathbf{V}=softmax(QK⊤/dk​​)V, each token's output a convex combination of value vectors. It is permutation-equivariant, so positions must be injected.
  • The 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_k}1/dk​​ factor keeps the logit variance at 1 (the raw variance is dkd_kdk​), preventing softmax saturation and vanishing gradients at initialization.
  • Multi-head attention splits ddd into hhh subspaces by view + transpose: tensors are (B, h, T, d_k) and the score tensor is (B, h, T, T). Heads are merged and mixed by WO\mathbf{W}_OWO​.
  • Block = communication + computation: attention moves information between tokens, the FFN (about two thirds of the parameters, 8d28d^28d2) transforms each token, and residual connections form the stream both write to.
  • Pre-norm (with RMSNorm) keeps an identity path and trains stably; post-norm needs warmup and care.
  • Position: sinusoidal and learned absolute vectors are added at the input; relative biases, RoPE (rotate Q,K\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K}Q,K so scores depend on n−mn-mn−m) and ALiBi act on the scores. RoPE is the modern default, with scaling for longer contexts.
  • Architectures differ by mask: encoder-only (full), decoder-only (causal), encoder-decoder (full + causal + cross). The causal mask enables parallel training and requires a KV cache for fast generation.
  • Cost: a layer is 24nd2+4n2d24nd^2+4n^2d24nd2+4n2d FLOPs; parameters ≈12Ld2\approx12Ld^2≈12Ld2; training ≈6ND\approx6ND≈6ND. The quadratic term bites beyond n≈6dn\approx6dn≈6d and in memory first. FlashAttention (exact), GQA and KV caching are the baseline fixes; sparse and linear variants are approximations with trade-offs.
  • Training recipe: AdamW with β2≈0.95\beta_2\approx0.95β2​≈0.95, linear warmup then cosine decay, gradient clipping, bf16 mixed precision (fp16 needs loss scaling), weight decay on matrices only, scaled residual-output init.

Further reading

  • (Essential) Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser, Polosukhin. "Attention Is All You Need." NeurIPS 2017 (arXiv:1706.03762).
  • (Essential) Jay Alammar, "The Illustrated Transformer" (blog, 2018): the best visual walkthrough.
  • (Essential) Andrej Karpathy, "Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out" (video, 2023) and the nanoGPT repository.
  • Elhage et al. "A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits." Anthropic, 2021: the residual-stream view.
  • Xiong et al. "On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture." ICML 2020 (arXiv:2002.04745): pre-norm versus post-norm.
  • Su, Lu, Pan, Murtadha, Wen, Liu. "RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding." 2021 (arXiv:2104.09864).
  • Press, Smith, Lewis. "Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation." ICLR 2022 (arXiv:2108.12409).
  • Shaw, Uszkoreit, Vaswani. "Self-Attention with Relative Position Representations." NAACL 2018.
  • Dao, Fu, Ermon, Rudra, Ré. "FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness." NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv:2205.14135).
  • Katharopoulos, Vyas, Pappas, Fleuret. "Transformers are RNNs: Fast Autoregressive Transformers with Linear Attention." ICML 2020 (arXiv:2006.16236).
  • Child, Gray, Radford, Sutskever. "Generating Long Sequences with Sparse Transformers." 2019 (arXiv:1904.10509); Beltagy, Peters, Cohan. "Longformer." 2020 (arXiv:2004.05150).
  • Zhang, Sennrich. "Root Mean Square Layer Normalization." NeurIPS 2019; Shazeer. "GLU Variants Improve Transformer." 2020 (arXiv:2002.05202).
  • Geva, Schuster, Berant, Levy. "Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories." EMNLP 2021.
  • Radford et al. "Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners" (GPT-2), 2019; Micikevicius et al. "Mixed Precision Training." ICLR 2018.
